etymology: A biblical title and figure of Christ as the immovable foundation and the smitten Rock that gave water (1 Cor 10:4).
biblical_def: The Rock is a great biblical figure of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is at once the immovable foundation on which His church is built and the smitten Rock from which the water of life flows. Paul declares of Israel in the wilderness that they did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ. The rock at Horeb, which Moses smote and from which water gushed to a thirsting people, was a type of Christ smitten on the cross, from whose riven side flow the living waters that quench the soul’s thirst for ever. Christ is also the Rock of foundation: other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ; the wise man builds his house upon the rock, and when the floods come it stands, for it is founded upon a rock. He is the chief corner stone, elect, precious, and the stone the builders rejected, become the head of the corner. The Rock speaks of His unchanging strength, His sure foundation, and His life-giving sacrifice. The dictionary honors Christ as the Rock—the smitten Rock who pours out living water, and the unmovable foundation on whom the church and the believing soul are safely built—against the shifting sands of every other refuge, that the man who builds on Him shall never be moved.
webster_summary: A figure of Christ as the smitten Rock that gives living water and the immovable foundation on whom the church is built; that Rock was Christ.

corruption_summary: The Rock is reduced to mere metaphor of stability, or wrongly applied to Peter; Scripture makes Christ the smitten Rock of living water and the church’s one foundation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors attend the figure of the Rock. The first reduces it to a vague metaphor of stability—God as a comforting symbol of steadiness—detached from the smitten Rock of the cross and the personal Christ. The second, the Roman error, applies the rock on which Christ builds His church to Peter and his supposed successors, making a man and an office the foundation, when the apostle himself confesses the foundation to be Christ: other foundation can no man lay (1 Cor 3:11).

The principle to recover is that Christ Himself is the Rock, in two great senses. He is the smitten Rock: as Moses struck the rock and water flowed to the thirsting people, so Christ was smitten on the cross, and that Rock was Christ (1 Cor 10:4), pouring out the living water that quenches the soul for ever. And He is the foundation Rock: the wise man builds upon the rock, and his house stands when the floods come (Matt 7:24); the LORD is the believer’s rock, fortress, and high tower (Psa 18:2). Against every shifting sand of human refuge, the believer builds on Christ alone, and is never moved.

etymology: From Psalm 95:1 and Deuteronomy 32; a title of the LORD as the strong, faithful ground of His people’s deliverance.
biblical_def: The Rock of our salvation is a title of the LORD as the strong, faithful, and unchanging ground of His people’s deliverance. The psalmist calls the people to worship: O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. The Song of Moses extols Him: He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he. The title gathers up several truths: the LORD is a rock for strength, an unshakable refuge in whom His people take shelter from every storm; a rock for stability, the unchanging God who is the same yesterday, today, and for ever; and a rock for salvation, the sure foundation of their deliverance, who has wrought their redemption and will not let it fail. Against the rock of the LORD, the gods of the nations are no rock at all, as Moses sang: their rock is not as our Rock. In the New Testament this Rock is revealed as Christ, the horn of salvation raised up for His people. The dictionary honors the Rock of our salvation as a name of comfort and confidence: that the believer’s deliverance rests not upon the sand of his own strength but upon the strong, faithful, eternal God, whose work is perfect and whose salvation cannot be moved.
webster_summary: A title of the LORD as the strong, faithful, unchanging ground of His people’s deliverance; the Rock whose work is perfect, revealed in Christ.

corruption_summary: Salvation’s ground is shifted to human strength or effort; Scripture names the LORD the Rock of our salvation, the strong and faithful ground that cannot be moved.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the perennial instinct to shift the ground of salvation from the LORD to ourselves—to rest deliverance on our own strength, resolve, or works, building on the sand of human ability rather than the Rock. Every such refuge fails when the storm comes; the gods of the nations and the idols of the self are no rock, as Moses sang, their rock is not as our Rock.

The principle to recover is that the LORD Himself is the Rock of our salvation, the strong and faithful ground that cannot be moved. He is the Rock, His work is perfect, and all His ways are judgment (Deu 32:4): His salvation is no half-finished, failing thing, but a perfect work. He only is the believer’s rock and salvation, his defence; he shall not be greatly moved (Psa 62:2). So the psalmist calls the people to worship Him with joy: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation (Psa 95:1). This Rock is revealed in Christ, the horn of salvation; and the believer who builds his hope upon Him, and not upon himself, stands secure when every other ground gives way.

etymology: From Acts 3:15; a title of Christ as the Author and Originator of life, whom men killed yet God raised.
biblical_def: The Prince of life is a title of the Lord Jesus Christ given by Peter in his sermon at the temple gate: And killed the Prince of life, whom God hath raised from the dead; whereof we are witnesses. The word translated Prince means the author, the originator, the captain, the one who leads and from whom a thing proceeds; Christ is the Prince of life as the very Author and Source of life, both the natural life by which all things live and move and have their being, and the eternal life He gives to His people. The title carries a sharp and holy irony, which Peter presses upon his hearers: they killed the Prince of life—the very Author of life put to death by His creatures; yet death could not hold its Lord, and God raised Him from the dead. The One who is life cannot be conquered by death; rather, by His death and rising He has abolished death and brought life and immortality to light. He has the keys of death and of hell, and gives eternal life to whomsoever He will. The dictionary honors Christ as the Prince of life—the Author of all life, whom wicked hands crucified, but whom God raised, the conqueror of death and the giver of life to His people—and presses the same wonder Peter pressed: that men should kill the Author of life, and that the slain Prince should rise to give life to His murderers who repent.
webster_summary: A title of Christ as the Author and Source of life, whom men killed yet God raised; the conqueror of death who gives eternal life to His people.

corruption_summary: Christ’s title is dimmed to mere honorific; Scripture proclaims Him the very Author of life, slain yet risen, the conqueror of death and giver of eternal life.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the dimming of the title into a mere honorific—Prince of life as a pious flourish—losing the staggering claim it makes. Peter does not flatter; he confronts. He charges his hearers that they killed the Prince of life (Acts 3:15): the very Author of life, the One in whom was life and the life was the light of men (John 1:4), was put to death by the creatures who owed Him their every breath. The title is a thunderclap, not an ornament.

The principle to recover is the deity and life-giving power of Christ, vindicated in His resurrection. The Author of life could not be held by death; God raised Him, and He is alive for evermore, holding the keys of hell and of death (Rev 1:18). He is Himself the resurrection and the life (John 11:25), and gives eternal life to whom He will. The wonder Peter pressed remains: that men should murder the Prince of life, and that the slain Prince should rise to offer life to His very murderers, if they repent. To confess Christ as the Prince of life is to bow before Him as the divine Source of all life and the conqueror of the grave.

etymology: From Luke 1:32; the title given to Christ by the angel Gabriel at the annunciation.
biblical_def: Son of the Highest is the title given to the Lord Jesus by the angel Gabriel at the annunciation, when he announced to Mary the conception of her son: He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David. The Highest, in the Scriptures, is a name of God Most High, the LORD who is exalted above all; and to call Jesus the Son of the Highest is to confess His true and proper deity, that He is the eternal Son of God Most High, of one substance with the Father. Gabriel joins to this title the promise of David’s throne and an everlasting kingdom: He shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end—so that the Son of the Highest is also the Son of David, the promised King. The same title is echoed when John the Baptist is called the prophet of the Highest, who goes before the face of the Lord; and the deity of the Son shines the brighter beside the prophet who only prepares His way. The dictionary honors the title Son of the Highest as a confession of the deity of Christ at His very conception—the eternal Son of God Most High, made flesh in the womb of the virgin, given the throne of David and an everlasting kingdom—that the church may worship the Babe of Bethlehem as the Son of the Highest, very God of very God.
webster_summary: Gabriel’s title for Christ at the annunciation; a confession of His true deity as the eternal Son of God Most High, given David’s throne and an everlasting kingdom.

corruption_summary: The title is read as mere honorific or adoptionist sonship; Scripture confesses Christ the true eternal Son of God Most High, deity from His conception.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is twofold and ancient. Some read Son of the Highest as a mere honorific, a title of dignity without the confession of deity; others fall into the adoptionist error, that Jesus became God’s Son at some point by exaltation, rather than being the eternal Son. But Gabriel’s words confess true deity from the conception: that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35); even the unclean spirits owned Him as the Son of the most high God (Mark 5:7).

The principle to recover is the deity of Christ from His very conception. The Highest is God Most High; the Son of the Highest is the eternal Son, of one substance with the Father, made flesh in the virgin’s womb by the power of the Highest overshadowing her (Luke 1:35). To this confession of deity Gabriel joins the promise of David’s throne and an everlasting kingdom: He shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of His kingdom there shall be no end (Luke 1:33). So the church worships the Babe of Bethlehem not as a creature merely honoured but as the Son of the Highest, very God of very God, the eternal Son made man for our salvation.

etymology: From Colossians 2:17 and Hebrews 10:1; the relation of the Old Testament types (shadow) to Christ (substance, body).
biblical_def: Shadow and substance names the great relation between the types and ordinances of the Old Testament and their fulfilment in Christ. Paul writes that the feasts, new moons, and sabbaths of the law are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ—the Greek soma, the body or substance that casts the shadow. The writer to the Hebrews says the law had a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things. A shadow is real, but it is not the thing itself; it is cast by a body and points to it, having its shape but not its substance. So the sacrifices, the priesthood, the tabernacle, the feasts, and the whole ceremonial law were shadows—true, God-given, and meaningful—cast by the coming Christ, who is the substance. They taught and pointed to Him: the lamb to the Lamb of God, the priest to the great High Priest, the temple to His body, the passover to His sacrifice. Now that the substance has come, the shadows have served their purpose and passed away; to cling to them is to prefer the shadow to the body, the picture to the person. The dictionary honors this distinction as a key to reading the Old Testament: its types are not abolished as worthless but fulfilled as shadows in the substance, Christ; and the believer, having the body, no longer walks among the shadows, but beholds the Lord to whom they all pointed.

corruption_summary: The types are either dismissed as worthless or clung to as still binding; Scripture holds them real shadows, fulfilled and passed in Christ the substance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two opposite errors mishandle shadow and substance. The first dismisses the Old Testament types as worthless relics, severing the shadows from the body and so losing the rich testimony they bear to Christ. The second clings to the shadows as still binding—reviving the ceremonial law, the sacrifices, a sacrificing priesthood, the feasts—as though the substance had not yet come, preferring the picture to the Person it portrays.

The principle to recover is that the types are real shadows, God-given and meaningful, now fulfilled and passed in Christ the substance. The feasts and ordinances were a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ (Col 2:17); the law had a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image (Heb 10:1). The shadow is cast by the body and shaped like it: the lamb pointed to the Lamb of God, the priest to the great High Priest, the tabernacle made according to the heavenly pattern (Heb 8:5) to the true tabernacle. The Scriptures testify of Christ (John 5:39). Now that He is come, the believer no longer walks among the shadows but beholds the substance; the types are honoured as fulfilled, not revived as binding.

etymology: From Psalm 118:22; the stone which the builders refused, become the head of the corner—a figure of Christ.
biblical_def: The rejected stone is the figure of Psalm 118, taken up by Christ and the apostles as a prophecy of His rejection and exaltation: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner. This is the LORD’s doing; it is marvellous in our eyes. The builders are the rulers of Israel, who examined the living Stone and cast Him away as unfit, crucifying the Lord of glory; yet the very stone they rejected God made the head of the corner, the chief and indispensable stone that binds the whole building together. The Lord applied the psalm to Himself before His enemies: Did ye never read in the scriptures, The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner? Peter preached it to the rulers: This is the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner; neither is there salvation in any other. The same Stone is precious to believers but, to the disobedient, a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, on which they fall and are broken. The dictionary honors the rejected stone as a great prophecy of Christ crucified and risen—refused by men, exalted by God, the head of the corner and the only foundation of salvation—and a solemn warning, that the Stone men reject in unbelief becomes the rock on which they are finally broken.

corruption_summary: The prophecy is reduced to a tale of unlikely success; Scripture proclaims Christ rejected by men and exalted by God, precious to faith and a stumbling-stone to unbelief.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the flattening of the prophecy into a mere proverb of unlikely success—the underdog vindicated, the overlooked one who rises—detached from its true subject, Christ crucified and risen. The psalm is no general maxim; it is a specific prophecy of the Messiah whom Israel’s builders examined and refused, and whom God exalted as the head of the corner. This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes (Matt 21:42).

The principle to recover is the double significance of the rejected Stone. To those who believe He is precious, the chief corner stone, the sure foundation, the head that binds the whole building—and neither is there salvation in any other, for this is the stone set at nought of the builders, become the head of the corner (Acts 4:11). But to the disobedient the same Stone is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence (1 Pet 2:7-8): they reject Him in unbelief, and on the very Stone they refuse they are at last broken. So the rejected Stone is both the only foundation of salvation and the rock of judgment; what men do with Him in rejection or faith determines whether He is their corner stone or their stumbling stone.

etymology: From Revelation 19:7; the consummation of the union between Christ the Lamb and His bride, the church.
biblical_def: The marriage of the Lamb is the glorious consummation, at the end of the age, of the union between Christ the Lamb and His bride, the church. John hears the voice of a great multitude in heaven crying, Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready. And to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints. The whole of Scripture has been a betrothal: the LORD took Israel to Himself as a husband; Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her, that He might sanctify and cleanse her, and present her to Himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing. The marriage supper of the Lamb is the wedding feast of that union made perfect—the everlasting joy of the redeemed in the immediate presence of their Lord, the bride forever with her Husband. Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. The dictionary honors the marriage of the Lamb as the great hope and end of the church’s history: that the Bridegroom who purchased His bride with His own blood will at last receive her to Himself, perfected and arrayed in His righteousness, to dwell with Him in unbroken joy for ever—the consummation toward which the whole story of redemption moves.

corruption_summary: The marriage of the Lamb is reduced to mere symbol or sentimental imagery; Scripture proclaims the real consummation of Christ’s blood-bought union with His church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the reduction of the marriage of the Lamb to mere symbol or sentimental imagery, emptied of its reality and its glory—a poetic flourish rather than the actual consummation toward which all redemption moves. But John heard the great multitude in heaven rejoice that the marriage of the Lamb is come (Rev 19:7); it is a real and coming event, the wedding of the Bridegroom and His bride, attested as the true sayings of God (Rev 19:9).

The principle to recover is the covenantal, blood-bought reality of Christ’s union with His church, perfected at the last. From the beginning the LORD has been Husband to His people; Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it, that He might present her to Himself a glorious church without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:25-27). The marriage of the Lamb is that purpose brought to its consummation: the bride arrayed in fine linen, the righteousness of saints; the holy city coming down prepared as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev 21:2); the redeemed forever with their Lord. It is the great hope and end of the church’s history—not a sentiment but a certainty, toward which the whole story of redemption presses, and in which the Bridegroom shall at last receive His bride to unbroken joy for ever.

etymology: From Revelation 6:16; the holy anger of Christ the Lamb against the impenitent in the day of judgment.
biblical_def: The wrath of the Lamb is the holy and dreadful anger of Christ against sin and the impenitent in the day of judgment—a phrase of awful weight, joining the gentlest of titles to the most terrible of realities. In the vision of the sixth seal, the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich, and every bond and free man hide themselves in the dens and rocks of the mountains, crying to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: for the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand? The same Christ who was led as a lamb to the slaughter, the Lamb of God who bore the sin of the world, is also the Lamb whose wrath the impenitent cannot endure; the meekness of His first coming gives way to the majesty of His judgment. The phrase rebukes the sentimental error that imagines a Christ all gentleness and no severity, who will judge no one; for the Lamb who was slain is also the Lion of the tribe of Judah, and His wrath against unrepented sin is the wrath of infinite holiness and love despised. The dictionary honors the wrath of the Lamb as a solemn revelation of the judgment of Christ—that the Saviour rejected becomes the Judge, and that there is no refuge from His wrath but in the blood of the Lamb Himself—and presses the only escape: to flee now to the Lamb slain, before the day of His wrath is come.
webster_summary: The holy anger of Christ the Lamb against the impenitent in the day of judgment; the meek Saviour rejected becomes the Judge, from whose wrath none can stand but in His blood.

corruption_summary: A sentimental religion denies that Christ has wrath at all; Scripture reveals the Lamb whose holy anger against the impenitent none can withstand but in His blood.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the sentimental religion of the age, which fashions a Christ all gentleness and no severity—a Saviour who saves but never judges, a Lamb with no wrath. But Scripture sets the very phrase wrath of the Lamb (Rev 6:16) against this fond delusion: the impenitent cry for the mountains to fall on them and hide them from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of His wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand? (Rev 6:17). The gentlest title is joined to the most terrible reality.

The principle to recover is that the meek Saviour rejected becomes the righteous Judge, and that His wrath is real and inescapable. The Lamb who was slain for sinners is also the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev 5:5), and the wrath of God abideth on every one who believes not the Son (John 3:36). His anger is no petulant temper but the wrath of infinite holiness and despised love, the just recoil of the holy God against unrepented sin. And here is the gospel hidden in the terror: there is no refuge from the wrath of the Lamb but in the blood of the Lamb. The only escape from His judgment is to flee, now, to Christ slain—before the great day of His wrath is come.

etymology: From Ephesians 6:12 and Colossians 2:15; the ranks of spiritual powers, especially the fallen angelic foes of the believer.
biblical_def: Principalities and powers is a phrase for the ranks and orders of spiritual beings, used in Scripture both of the angelic hierarchy and especially of the fallen spiritual foes against whom the believer wrestles. Paul writes that we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places—naming the unseen hosts of the devil, organized and mighty, as the church’s true enemies. Against these the believer is armed with the whole armour of God. Yet the same phrase proclaims the triumph of Christ: having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it—for on the cross Christ disarmed and led captive the very powers of darkness, as a conqueror leads his vanquished foes in his train. He is set far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion; all things are put under His feet; and not even principalities nor powers can separate the believer from the love of God in Christ. The dictionary honors this phrase as a sober witness to the reality of unseen spiritual conflict—that the believer’s war is not merely against human enemies but against organized hosts of darkness—and as a triumphant proclamation that Christ has conquered these powers at the cross, set them under His feet, and secured His people, so that they fight a defeated foe in the strength of a victorious Lord.

corruption_summary: The spiritual powers are either denied as superstition or reimagined as mere social structures; Scripture names real spiritual foes, conquered by Christ at the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond two errors. The first denies the principalities and powers altogether, dismissing them as ancient superstition—a worldview the enlightened may discard. But Paul, by the Spirit, names them as real: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against spiritual wickedness in high places (Eph 6:12). The second error, common in some modern theology, reimagines the powers as mere impersonal social or political structures—systems of oppression—emptying them of their personal, spiritual, demonic reality. Scripture knows them as organized hosts of fallen spirits, not abstractions.

The principle to recover is the reality of spiritual conflict and the completeness of Christ’s triumph. The believer’s true war is against unseen and mighty foes, for which he must take the whole armour of God. Yet these foes are already conquered: on the cross Christ spoiled principalities and powers, and made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them (Col 2:15); He is set far above all principality and power (Eph 1:21), and all things are under His feet. Therefore neither principalities nor powers can separate the believer from the love of God in Christ (Rom 8:38). The Christian fights a defeated enemy in the strength of a victorious Lord—sober about the conflict, yet certain of the outcome.

etymology: Greek Apollyon, the destroyer; the angel of the bottomless pit, called in Hebrew Abaddon (Rev 9:11).
biblical_def: Apollyon is the name given in the Revelation to the angel of the bottomless pit—in Hebrew, Abaddon; in Greek, Apollyon—both meaning the Destroyer. And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon, but in the Greek tongue hath his name Apollyon. The name reveals the character of Satan and his hosts: they are destroyers, whose work is ruin and death, for the devil was a murderer from the beginning, a thief who comes but to steal, and to kill, and to destroy. Apollyon is set in sharp contrast to Christ: the Destroyer against the Saviour, the one who kills against the one who gives life abundantly. In Bunyan’s great allegory, Apollyon meets Christian in the Valley of Humiliation and, straddling the whole breadth of the way, does battle with him; and Christian, sorely wounded, prevails at last by the sword of the Spirit and the blood of the Lamb, crying, Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. The dictionary honors the name Apollyon as a revelation of the destroying nature of the enemy of souls—not a harmless figure of folklore but a real and malignant destroyer—and as a summons to the believer’s warfare: that the Destroyer is met and overcome not by the strength of man but by Christ the Saviour, who came to destroy the works of the devil, and through whom His people are more than conquerors.

corruption_summary: Apollyon is dismissed as folklore or the devil denied altogether; Scripture reveals a real destroyer, overcome only by Christ and the blood of the Lamb.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the dismissal of Apollyon as mere folklore, or the wider denial of the devil altogether—the comfortable modern unbelief that there is no personal adversary, no destroyer, no real spiritual enemy of the soul. But Scripture names him: the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name is Abaddon, Apollyon, the Destroyer (Rev 9:11); and the Lord Himself describes the thief who comes but to steal, and to kill, and to destroy (John 10:10). To deny the Destroyer is to disarm the believer before a real and malignant foe.

The principle to recover is the destroying nature of the enemy and the conquering work of Christ. Apollyon’s very name declares his work: ruin, death, destruction; he was a murderer from the beginning. But the Son of God was manifested for this purpose, that He might destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8)—the Saviour against the Destroyer, the Lifegiver against the murderer. And the saints overcome him not by their own strength but by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony, loving not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11). As Bunyan’s Christian prevailed over Apollyon in the Valley of Humiliation, so the believer, sorely pressed, is yet more than conqueror through Him that loved him.
